meaning.evidence: All facts kept: the 227-year-old hemlock, 1791, "gusts of reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 km/h)", the whisky barrel, Clinton not related, VP 1805–1812, the magnolia and the sequoia. "with bits set aside for special projects" and "delivered in a whisky barrel, no less" are colour on original points.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "got knocked flat on Friday by gusts", "Washington's own patch", "as a pressie", "It's not the only old US tree to come a gutser lately" (a heavy fall, apt for a toppled tree). "governments" for administrations is a fair Aussie rendering.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Aussie telling the story: "the Mount Vernon mob", "come a gutser", "pressie", "cos the first White House wasn't built yet". "So get this." is a slightly stock opener.

register.evidence: Right at level 3: a steady sprinkle of Aussie through the piece ("own patch", "mob", "pressie", "no less", "come a gutser") without turning it into a pub yarn. No swearing.

tone.evidence: Keeps the light, curious news-item tone, a touch chattier: "And no, the New York governor's no relation to the 42nd President Bill Clinton".

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout: "The hemlock went in back in 1791, and it got knocked flat on Friday by gusts of reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 km/h)."

variety.evidence: Varied: "taken out", "knocked flat", "patch", "mob", "pressie", "no less", "come a gutser"; nothing repeated.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the same story of the fallen Mount Vernon hemlock and its history, retold: "It was sent down by New York Governor George Clinton as a pressie, delivered in a whisky barrel, no less."

problems.why: Added stock opener; fine as colour but a little forced.

problems.quote: According to the Mount Vernon mob
problems.why: "Mob" for estate officials is natural Aussie but a touch cheeky for officials.

A.summary: The best-judged level-3 retelling: faithful, smooth, varied and genuinely Australian.

meaning.evidence: All facts kept: "gathered up to be preserved and put towards special projects", "reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 kph)", the barrel, the Clinton note, the other fallen trees.

sense.evidence: Mostly fits: "own place", "as a pressie", "it rocked up in a whisky barrel". "the people running the Mount Vernon estate reckoned the Canadian hemlock had been gathered up" makes a factual report sound like an opinion.

authenticity.evidence: Natural where used: "cos the first White House wasn't finished yet", "it rocked up in a whisky barrel", "no relation". Nothing forced.

register.evidence: A little light for level 3: a handful of terms ("reckoned", "pressie", "rocked up", "cos") over mostly plain retelling. No swearing.

tone.evidence: Keeps the newsy, mildly curious tone: "It's not the only bit of US history to come down lately, either."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly: "The hemlock went in the ground in 1791 and came down in Friday's gusts, which were reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 kph)."

variety.evidence: Modest range; "come down" and "came down" do double duty for falling ("came down in Friday's gusts", "to come down lately").

essence.evidence: Clearly the same story with its distinctive whisky-barrel and Clinton details: "it rocked up in a whisky barrel".

B.summary: Faithful, smooth and natural, slightly lighter than level 3, with one strained "reckoned".

meaning.evidence: All facts kept, including "used for special projects", "gusts reportedly up to 70 mph (about 110 kph)", "it turned up in a whisky barrel", and the Clinton and other-trees details.
